text: Massive hemorrhage, extremity: apply a CoTCCC-recommended limb tourniquet for life-threatening extremity bleeding or traumatic amputation. In Care Under Fire place it high and tight over the uniform; in Tactical Field Care, if the first tourniquet does not stop bleeding or eliminate the distal pulse, tighten it or place a second tourniquet side by side just above the first. Record the time of application on the tourniquet and the casualty card.

Tourniquet reassessment and conversion: expose the wound and reassess every tourniquet. Convert a hasty high-and-tight tourniquet to a deliberate one 2-3 inches above the wound when tactically feasible. Attempt conversion to a hemostatic or pressure dressing within 2 hours of application if the casualty is not in shock, can be monitored, and the tourniquet is not on an amputated limb. Do not remove a tourniquet that has been on for more than 6 hours unless close monitoring and lab capability are available.

Compressible (junctional) hemorrhage not amenable to limb tourniquet — groin, axilla, neck: pack the wound with CoTCCC-recommended hemostatic dressing (e.g., Combat Gauze) and apply at least 3 minutes of direct pressure, then a pressure bandage. If the site is suitable, apply a junctional tourniquet. Reassess for re-bleeding after every casualty movement.

Airway: an unconscious casualty without airway obstruction may be placed in the recovery position; consider a nasopharyngeal airway (NPA) for casualties with altered mental status. A conscious casualty with an airway injury should be allowed to assume the position that best protects the airway, including sitting up and leaning forward. If the airway is obstructed or obstruction is imminent and other measures fail, perform a surgical cricothyroidotomy with lidocaine if the casualty is conscious.

Respiration — suspected tension pneumothorax: suspect it in a casualty with torso trauma or primary blast injury and progressive respiratory distress, falling SpO2, absent breath sounds on one side, or traumatic cardiac arrest. Decompress with a 14-gauge 3.25-inch needle/catheter at the 5th intercostal space anterior axillary line or the 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line. Repeat or try the alternate site if symptoms recur.

Open or sucking chest wound: immediately apply a vented chest seal (or a non-vented seal if vented is unavailable). Monitor for developing tension pneumothorax; if it develops, burp or remove the seal and/or perform needle decompression. Monitor SpO2 if a pulse oximeter is available and give supplemental oxygen when available.

Circulation — shock assessment and access: signs of hemorrhagic shock include altered mental status in the absence of brain injury and/or a weak or absent radial pulse. Reassess prior bleeding-control measures. Establish IV or IO access if resuscitation or medications are needed. Whole blood is the preferred resuscitation fluid; give in 1-unit increments until a palpable radial pulse, improved mental status, or systolic BP of roughly 100 mmHg (110 for TBI).

Tranexamic acid (TXA): give TXA as soon as possible, and within 3 hours of injury, to a casualty who will likely need a blood transfusion — e.g., hemorrhagic shock, one or more major amputations, penetrating torso trauma, or evidence of severe bleeding — or with signs of significant TBI. Current CoTCCC guidance is 2 grams by slow IV/IO push. Do not give TXA beyond 3 hours after injury.

Hypothermia prevention: take early and aggressive steps to prevent heat loss in every casualty, especially those in shock. Minimise exposure to cold ground, wind and air; replace wet clothing; place the casualty on an insulated surface; use an active heating blanket and a hypothermia prevention kit (e.g., HPMK) or improvised wraps; keep the head covered; warm resuscitation fluids when possible.

Head injury (the H in MARCH-PAWS also covers head injury / TBI): prevent hypoxia and hypotension, target SpO2 above 90 percent and adequate blood pressure, elevate the head about 30 degrees if not in shock, monitor for unequal pupils and decreasing level of consciousness, and document AVPU or GCS serially. Consider TXA for significant TBI within 3 hours.

Pain management (MARCH-PAWS): for mild-to-moderate pain in a casualty still able to fight, use the combat wound medication pack (acetaminophen and meloxicam). For moderate-to-severe pain in a casualty not in shock, consider oral transmucosal fentanyl (OTFC) 800 mcg. For casualties in or at risk of shock, use ketamine: 20-30 mg IV/IO slow push or 50-100 mg IM/IN, repeat as needed. Monitor airway and breathing after opioid or ketamine use; have naloxone available.

Antibiotics for open combat wounds: if able to take oral medication, give moxifloxacin 400 mg by mouth once daily. If unable to take oral medication (shock, unconsciousness, penetrating abdominal trauma), give ertapenem 1 g IV/IM once daily or ceftriaxone 2 g IV/IM once daily. Check and dress wounds and splint fractures.

Burns: facial burns, especially from closed-space fires, may be associated with inhalation injury — monitor airway closely and consider early surgical airway if respiratory distress develops. Estimate total body surface area burned to the nearest 10 percent using the rule of nines, cover with dry sterile dressings, and use hypothermia prevention measures. Fluid resuscitation is indicated for burns over 20 percent TBSA.

CPR in the tactical setting: CPR for victims of blast or penetrating trauma who have no pulse, no ventilations and no other signs of life will not be successful and should not be attempted in Care Under Fire. In Tactical Field Care, consider bilateral needle decompression for a casualty with torso trauma or polytrauma and no respirations or pulse before discontinuing care, to ensure tension pneumothorax is not the cause of the arrest.

Documentation and reassessment: document clinical assessments, treatments rendered and changes in the casualty's status on a DD Form 1380 TCCC Card and forward it with the casualty. Reassess and record vital signs serially (pulse rate and location, blood pressure, respiratory rate, SpO2, AVPU, pain scale), especially after every intervention and every movement of the casualty.
